syllabusTopics: Saturated hydrocarbons (Alkanes): preparation from haloalkanes (reduction and Wurtz reaction), decarboxylation, catalytic hydrogenation of alkene and alkyne
Chemical properties of alkanes: substitution reactions (halogenation, nitration and sulphonation only), oxidation of ethane
Unsaturated hydrocarbons (Alkenes): preparation by dehydration of alcohol, dehydrohalogenation, catalytic hydrogenation of alkyne
Chemical properties of alkenes: addition reaction with HX (Markovnikov's addition and peroxide effect), H2O, O3, H2SO4 only
Alkynes: preparation from carbon and hydrogen, 1,2-dibromoethane, chloroform/iodoform only
Chemical properties of alkynes: addition reaction with H2, HX, H2O; acidic nature (action with sodium, ammoniacal AgNO3 and ammoniacal Cu2Cl2)
Test of unsaturation (ethene and ethyne): bromine water test and Baeyer's test
Comparative studies of physical properties of alkane, alkene and alkyne
Kolbe's electrolysis methods for the preparation of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes

rows.text: Alkanes answer only to radicals and brute conditions. **Halogenation** is free-radical substitution under UV: initiation (**Cl₂ → 2Cl·**), propagation (**Cl· + CH₄ → CH₃· + HCl; CH₃· + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl·**), termination (radical combination) — the NEB 2020 mechanism, whose product mixture arises because CH₃Cl keeps reacting on to CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄.…

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Covers only: chemical properties of alkanes: substitution reactions, halogenation, nitration, sulphonation only (within Hydrocarbons).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Alkane halogenation is a free-radical chain substitution initiated by light; nitration and sulphonation require harsh vapour-phase or fuming-acid conditions."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***One photon, many products*** — a single UV photon splits one Cl2, yet thousands of CH3Cl molecules form: each propagation step regenerates the radical that drives the next.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Quiet Family Speaks Alkanes have only strong, non-polar C–C and C–H σ bonds, so they ignore ionic reagents and burn or substitute instead. Their chemistry is **free-radical substitution** (halogenation), plus harsh-condition **nitration**, **sulphonation**, and **combustion/oxidation** — with ethane's controlled oxidation as the set example.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Halogenation (free-radical substitution) - **CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl** (diffused sunlight/UV); continues: CH₂Cl₂ → CHCl₃ → CCl₄. - Mechanism: **initiation** (Cl₂ → 2Cl·), **propagation** (Cl· + CH₄ → CH₃· + HCl; CH₃· + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl·), **termination** (radical combination). - Reactivity of halogens: **F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂** (fluorine explodes; iodine is reversible).…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Chain: initiation (hν), propagation (×2), termination. Product ladder CH3Cl→CCl4. F>Cl>Br>I. Nitration 400 °C vapour. Sulphonation long-chain only. Ethane controlled oxidation → CH3CHO.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: No π bond means no ionic foothold: every alkane reaction is radical substitution or oxidation — conditions (UV, 400 °C vapour, fuming acid) supply the energy the σ bonds demand.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Alkanes: only radical substitution + harsh-condition reactions. Halogenation: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl (UV); chain continues to CH2Cl2, CHCl3, CCl4 (mixture); mechanism initiation Cl2 -> 2Cl., propagation Cl. + CH4 -> CH3. + HCl then CH3.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Bromine's selectivity (3° > 2° > 1° H) makes it the diagnostic halogen — chlorine is fast but careless, bromine is slow but choosy.

rows.text: Give equations for nitration of methane and controlled oxidation of ethane.  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **Substitution, not addition:** alkanes have nothing to add to; every halogenation replaces an H.  ·  **Nitration needs vapour phase:** aqueous HNO₃ does nothing to methane — the ~400 °C vapour reaction is the exam answer.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Iodination runs backwards:** HI reduces the alkyl iodide back, so I₂ halogenation needs HNO₃ or HIO₃ to remove HI.  ·  ## 7.
